The analysis is for laminar, constant-property, two-dimensional planar, boundary-layer-type flow without appreciable viscous dissipation.
The plate is idealized as a thin flat plate of thickness b with its lower surface exposed to coolant at a constant temperature Tc and a constant surface coefficient of heat transfer h.
The transient is initiated by a step change in the fluid inlet temperature from Tc to T∞ at time t = 0.
The exact analytical solution is obtained using two successive Laplace transformations.
The coupling parameter ε is a measure of the ratio of the thermal storage capacity of the boundary-layer fluid per unit length to the thermal storage capacity of the solid plate per unit length.
The parameter η is a measure of the ratio of the coolant-side surface coefficient to the local gas-side surface coefficient.
The transient solution does not exhibit infinite or very large heat fluxes at the beginning, unlike the transient induced by a step change in wall temperature.
A criterion is developed to determine the minimum value of the time parameter ε(τ-1) for which the solution is within 5% of the steady-state values.

For the case where the fluid and plate are initially at the steady-state conditions, the transient solution is obtained by decomposing the temperature into a steady-state component and a transient component.
The unit step function in the solution indicates that the surface heat flux and temperature are zero for τ < 1, and only attain nonzero values for τ ≥ 1.
The 'plane wave' phenomenon in slug flow refers to the separation of the thermal fluid field into two regions - conduction with no mixing ahead of the front, and mixing behind the front.
The eventual steady-state surface heat flux and temperature are independent of the coupling parameter ε and dependent only on the parameter η.
As ε approaches infinity, the plate has essentially zero thermal storage capacity compared to the fluid, and the surface heat flux is zero for τ < 1 and equal to its steady-state value for τ ≥ 1.
For η = 0, corresponding to an insulated lower surface, the steady-state surface heat flux and temperature are both zero.
The quasi-steady approximation can induce appreciable error, especially for short times, highlighting the importance of using the exact transient solution.
